Scripture didn't sand these men down, and God used them anyway, and their children watched all of it. That doesn't mean failure is small. David's sin cost his family dearly. It means God disciples people through truth about failure, not through the pretense of having none. A father who lets his children see him follow God, get it wrong, repent out loud and keep going is handing down something far more durable than a performance. He's showing them what to do when they fail, which they will.

So Joshua, an old man near the end of his life, stands before the whole nation and says, "Choose this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served in the region beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:15). He doesn't say his house has arrived. He sets a direction. A father's job isn't to be the faith. It's to point the house toward God and lead the way down the road, stumbling included. Your children don't need you to be God. They need to see you following him: praying, reading Scripture, saying you're sorry, giving when it costs, forgiving someone who didn't deserve it. Bonhoeffer, in The Cost of Discipleship, warned against cheap grace, grace that costs nothing and changes nothing. A father who only ever performs having arrived hands his children something close to it, a religion of appearances with no living root. Disciple them from inside your own discipleship instead.

I have five sons, and I write this as a fellow learner, not as a man who has finished. Which brings us to the hardest grace of fatherhood, the long view. You're planting a tree whose shade you may not sit in. Some of what you sow in a child won't surface for twenty years, and some of your best work you'll never see. A faith that goes quiet in a son's twenties can wake up years later over a crib of his own. Paul told the Corinthians, "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth" (1 Corinthians 3:6-7). That division of labor is a mercy to every father afraid he isn't enough. You aren't the one who makes it grow. You're the one who plants, waters and stays. And remember how Timothy's faith came to him: "a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well" (2 Timothy 1:5). It came down a chain of ordinary, named people, each faithful in their stretch of the road. Your faithfulness may surface not in your son but in a grandchild you never meet.

The long view brings one more freedom, freedom from comparison, which quietly poisons a lot of fathering. When you can't see the harvest, you're tempted to measure yourself against other men's visible results, the family whose children all walk with God, the father whose teenagers seem effortless, and to read your own struggles as proof you've failed. But you're seeing the surface of other homes and the depths of your own, comparing their best moments with your private knowledge of every place you fell short. That contest is rigged, and you'll always lose it. More than that, you're forgetting that the growth was never yours to produce. You have one assignment: be faithful in your stretch of the road with the children God actually gave you, and trust him with the outcome. Another father's harvest is between him and the God who gives the growth.

We end where we began, with the Father who runs. This whole study has been one argument. You can't give what you haven't received, and in Christ you've received a Father who delights in you, disciplines you in love, blesses you before you perform, and is patient with your unfinished faith. Go and be, by his mercy, a faint but real reflection of him to the children he's given you. There's no such thing as a finished father modeling a finished faith, and pretending to be one is its own quiet hypocrisy. What your children need is a truthful father, still in it, letting them watch him follow, fail, repent and keep going, planting what he won't live to see. It will be enough. Not because you are, but because he is.

scriptureStudy.note: "But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." A father sets the direction for his household. He doesn't claim to have arrived; he says which way the house will face and leads down that road.
Timothy's faith "dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice." Faith handed down through ordinary, named people. Your faithfulness may surface in a grandchild you never meet.
"I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth." The grower is God, which frees a father from believing the outcome rests on his performance.
The fathers are to teach their children "so that they should set their hope in God." The aim of all the telling is hope in God, not in the father. A father points past himself.

Joshua is told to be strong and courageous, because "It is the LORD who goes before you. He will be with you; he will not leave you or forsake you." A man leads a people, or a household, on the strength of a God who has gone ahead.

discussion.q: Has shame about your own failures kept you quiet about faith with your children? What would change if truthfulness, not perfection, were the standard?
discussion.behind: Name the real barrier. Most men aren't unbelieving; they feel disqualified. The gospel disqualifies the pretense, not the man.

discussion.q: When did your children last see you follow God in a way you didn't narrate, in prayer, repentance, generosity or forgiveness?
discussion.behind: Faith is largely caught. Help men find the unstaged moments their children are actually watching.

discussion.q: Read 1 Corinthians 3:5-9. What does it do to you to hear that you may not see the harvest of your best fathering?
discussion.behind: The long view is freeing and frightening. Let men sit with it. It releases the need for measurable results, and the despair when they don't come.

discussion.q: Read 2 Timothy 1:5. Timothy's faith passed from Lois to Eunice to him. Who handed the faith to you, and who are you handing it to? Name them out loud.
discussion.behind: Make the chain concrete. Some men received nothing and are the first link, and that's a calling of its own. Help each man find his place in the chain and name the next link.

discussion.q: Looking back over these five sessions, what's the one turn God is asking of you as a father?
discussion.behind: Drive toward one concrete repentance or commitment per man, not a list. One turn named out loud is worth more than five resolved in private.

objections.objection: If I talk about faith while failing this much, I'm just being a hypocrite.
objections.response: A hypocrite hides the failure and performs the virtue. A disciple admits the failure and follows anyway. Letting your children see you repent is the opposite of hypocrisy. It's one of the most truthful things a father can do, and it shows them what to do with their own failures. Silence, not candor, is what hands down a brittle faith.

objections.objection: My kids have already walked away from the faith. It's too late.
objections.response: The long view cuts both ways. You may not see the harvest, but you can't see the end of the story from here either. The father in Jesus' parable didn't chase his son into the far country; he watched the road. Faithful presence, an open door and prayer are never too late, because the one who gives the growth isn't finished. Augustine walked away from his mother's faith for years and came back. Monica prayed the whole time and lived to see it. Many faithful parents don't, and the coming back is no less real when a parent doesn't live to see it.

objections.objection: Faith should be a private matter. It isn't my place to impose my beliefs on my children; they should choose for themselves when they grow up.
objections.response: There's something right in this. Faith can't be forced, and a child does have to own it for himself. But no father is neutral, and claiming neutrality is itself a position your children will absorb. You're handing down a way of seeing the world every day, in what you spend on, worry about, celebrate and never mention. The question isn't whether you'll form your children but toward what. Staying silent about the deepest thing you believe, in the name of letting them choose, teaches them it isn't worth speaking of, and that's a conviction too. Joshua didn't coerce anyone. He said, "Choose this day whom you will serve," and named where his own house stood. A father who does that, and leaves his children truly free to wrestle with it, gives them more to choose from, not less.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What's the one turn God is asking of you as a father, and who will you tell so it doesn't stay a private thought?
sessions.practice: Do two things this week. First, let your children see one unstaged act of your own faith: pray in front of them, apologize to them, or give where it costs. Second, write down one hope you're planting in each child that you may not live to see, and give it to God in prayer.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father who runs, you've met us in our wounds, given us your presence, held discipline and tenderness together, blessed us before we performed, and been patient with our unfinished faith. Make us truthful fathers who point our children past ourselves to you. Let us plant what we won't sit under, and trust you for the growth we can't give. As for us and our houses, we will serve the Lord. Amen.
reflection: What has kept me quiet about faith with my children?
What unstaged act of faith can my children see in me this week?
Who handed the faith to me, and who am I handing it to?
What am I planting that I may never see, and can I trust it to God?

memoryVerse.text: And if it is evil in your eyes to serve the LORD, choose this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served in the region beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the long Christian sense of faithfulness across generations, because it speaks to the despair a father feels when he can't see results. When God names himself to Moses, he speaks of "keeping steadfast love for thousands" in the same breath as visiting iniquity "to the third and the fourth generation" (Exodus 34:7), and Moses later puts the promise as love "to a thousand generations" (Deuteronomy 7:9). The arithmetic isn't subtle. The mercy outruns the judgment by a long way. A father who feels he's failing should sit with that lopsided math.

Then look at the actual chains the Bible shows us. Lois to Eunice to Timothy. The fathers of Psalm 78, commanded to tell the next generation "that the next generation might know them, the children yet unborn, and arise and tell them to their children" (Psalm 78:6), a relay that runs past any one runner's sight of the finish. And read Augustine's Confessions on his mother Monica, who prayed for her wandering son for years with no evidence it was working, and whose prayers he later saw as heard all along by the God who was drawing him home. The discipline is to father for a harvest you won't measure: plant, keep the porch light on, and trust the growth to the only one who gives it.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a father in your group has an adult son who has walked away from the faith entirely. He won't come to church, he's openly dismissive of God, and the relationship is strained. The father is crushed and quietly blames himself, sure that some failure of his caused it, and he has nearly stopped praying because every prayer feels like proof he failed. He asks you directly whether it's too late, and whether there's any point in going on.

How would you answer him without promising that his son will come back, and without letting him collapse into a despair that gives up the long view? What does faithful fathering look like for a man whose harvest, if it comes, he may not live to see?

devotional.title: As For Me and My House
devotional.body:
Joshua is an old man near the end of his life, standing before the whole nation, and he sets a direction: "Choose this day whom you will serve... But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:15). Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say his house has arrived. He doesn't claim his children have it figured out or that he's finished the work. He says which way the house will face, and he leads down that road.

That's the freedom a shame-bound father needs. Your job isn't to be the faith, perfected and complete. Your job is to set the direction and lead, stumbling included. Joshua's declaration isn't a boast about his family's holiness. It's a commitment about the road they'll walk. You can make that declaration today, not because you've arrived, but because someone in the house has to say which way it faces. Stop waiting until you're good enough to lead. Set the direction and start walking.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I've been waiting to be a good enough example before I lead my house toward you, and that day won't come. Let me say today which way my house faces, and lead down that road, stumbling and all.

devotional.title: Lois and Eunice
devotional.body:
Paul reminds Timothy of "a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well" (2 Timothy 1:5). Stop and see what that sentence is: a chain. Faith handed down through three generations of ordinary, named people, each faithful in their own stretch of the road. Lois couldn't have known an apostle would one day write about the faith she passed to her daughter. She was faithful, in her time, with the child in front of her.

That's how faith usually travels, through chains of unremarkable faithfulness, one generation to the next. It should free you from believing everything depends on you and your results. You're one link. You received the faith, maybe from a named person, maybe from no one at all, and you're handing it on, and the harvest may show up in a grandchild you never meet. Be faithful in your stretch. That's the whole assignment, and it's enough.
devotional.prayer: Father, your faith travels down chains of ordinary people, from Lois to Eunice to Timothy. Make me faithful in my stretch of the road, and carry what I plant into generations I'll never see.

devotional.title: God Gave the Growth
devotional.body:
"I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth" (1 Corinthians 3:6-7). Read that as a father afraid he isn't enough, because it's aimed at you. The growing was never your job. You plant. You water. You stay. God, and only God, makes anything grow.

It's a mercy, though it may not feel like one when you're desperate to see results. We want to be the ones who make faith take root in our children, and when it doesn't visibly take, we conclude we've failed. But you can't make a seed grow by staring at the soil, and you can't make faith grow in a child by force of effort. You can be faithful with prayer, presence, a truthful example and an open door, and then hand the growth to the one who gives it. Today, take the child you're most anxious about and deliberately hand them back to God.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I plant and water and stay, but you alone give the growth. Free me from believing the harvest rests on my performance, and let me trust my children to you.

devotional.title: Tell the Next Generation
devotional.body:
The psalm tells the fathers to pass on "the glorious deeds of the LORD" (Psalm 78:4) so "that the next generation might know them, the children yet unborn, and arise and tell them to their children, so that they should set their hope in God" (Psalm 78:6-7). Notice where it lands. The aim of all the telling is hope in God. Not in the father, or the family name, or the tradition. The point of a father speaking the faith is to point his children past himself.

That should let you breathe out. You aren't the destination. You're a signpost, and a signpost that points at itself is broken. Your failures, which you know too well, aren't finally the issue, because you never asked your children to hope in you. You're pointing them past your own unfinished faith to a God who doesn't stumble. So speak. Tell them what God has done, in your own words, on an ordinary day, and trust that the telling works not by being flawless but by pointing to someone who is.
devotional.prayer: Father, the aim of all my telling is that my children would hope in you, not in me. Make me a signpost that points past my failures to the God who doesn't fail.

devotional.title: The Harvest Is Not Yours
devotional.body:
"When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. Then he said to his disciples, 'The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest'" (Matthew 9:36-38). Notice the title: the Lord of the harvest. The harvest belongs to him. Laborers labor; the Lord brings in the harvest. You're a laborer in your own home, sent into a field you didn't make, and the outcome rests with him.

This study ends where it began, with the Father who runs. You can't give what you haven't received, and in Christ you've received a Father who delights in you, disciplines you in love, blesses you before you perform, and is patient with your unfinished faith. Go and be, by his mercy, a faint but real reflection of him to the children he's given you. Plant what you won't live to sit under. Keep the porch light on. And trust the harvest to its Lord, who isn't finished yet.
devotional.prayer: Lord of the harvest, the children you gave me are a field I can't make grow. Make me a faithful laborer in my own home, planting what I may not see, and trusting you for the harvest that's yours to bring in. Amen.

leaderPrimer:
You agreed to lead a study on fatherhood, which means you're about to ask a room of men to talk about something many of them have spent a lifetime not talking about. Go in with your eyes open. Some men carry a father wound deep enough that the first session will reach places they've kept sealed for decades. Your job isn't to pry those places open. It's to make the room safe enough that a man can open them himself if he chooses, and to be unshockable when he does.

The most important thing you'll do is go first. When you speak truthfully about your own father and your own failures as a father, you give every other man permission to do the same. If you perform having it together, the room will perform right back, and nothing real will happen. This study is written by a fellow learner, not an expert, and that's the posture you're asked to lead from.

Watch the pace. These sessions move men toward grief, and grief can't be hurried. If a man goes quiet or his eyes fill, let the silence sit rather than filling it. Resist the urge to fix. A man who shares a wound doesn't need it solved in the next two minutes. He needs you to receive it and point him gently to the Father who runs. Be careful too with the man whose father was good, and with the man estranged from his own children; the study can cut in unexpected directions, and your warmth toward the edges of the room matters as much as how you handle the center.

You'll likely meet several kinds of men. There's the man wounded by absence or coldness, for whom session one is hardest. There's the dutiful older-brother man who never rebelled and is quietly starving for a blessing he never got, for whom session four cuts deepest. There's the hard father and the soft father, each fleeing the opposite ditch in session three. And there's the man whose grown children are walking away, for whom session five presses on a live grief; walk closely with him and follow up outside the meeting.

Finally, don't let the study end in conviction alone, which turns into shame. Every session moves from the wound or the failure to grace, and you have to make that turn out loud, every time, or men will go home heavier instead of freer. The goal isn't better fathers by willpower. It's men who have received the Father's love and finally have something to give.

faq.q: Is this only for fathers with young children?
faq.a: No. The father wound has no age limit, and neither does the call to bless and to repair. Fathers of adult children, grandfathers, estranged fathers and men who hope to be fathers one day all belong in the room. Several sessions deal with making peace with your own father, which any man can do, and session five speaks to the man whose harvest is decades out or whose grown children have wandered.

faq.q: What about men whose fathers were genuinely good?
faq.a: They belong here too, and the study will serve them differently. A man with a good father often carries a quiet fear of not measuring up, and he still needs to hear that his standing rests on the Father's delight rather than on matching his dad. Encourage him to take the sessions as gratitude and stewardship rather than grief, and to be tender toward the men for whom this is fresh pain rather than a fond memory.

faq.q: Can mothers, or single moms raising sons, use this?
faq.a: It's written to fathers, but a single mother raising sons, or a mentor, will find much of it useful for understanding the father hunger in the boys they love and for pointing them to the Father of the fatherless. Consider a parallel group, or inviting men in the church to step toward those boys. The study itself argues that God takes the title "Father of the fatherless" precisely for homes where a father is missing.

faq.q: One of our men is estranged from his children. Is this study going to wound him?
faq.a: It may bring up real grief, and you should be ready for that, but the study is built to meet it. The last session speaks directly to the father who fears it's too late, and the whole study moves toward the open door and the porch light rather than toward measurable results. Walk closely with him, follow up outside the meeting, and never let the room rush him toward a resolution that isn't his to force.

faq.q: How long should each session run?
faq.a: The plan assumes about ninety minutes. You can shorten it by dropping a discussion question, or split each session across two meetings at the natural break between the teaching and the quiet room. Don't cut the turn to grace to save time; cut a question instead. The daily devotionals between sessions keep the work going during the week, so the meeting doesn't have to carry everything.

faq.q: What are the devotional days for, and are they required?
faq.a: Each session has five short devotionals, one for each day between meetings, so the study keeps working on the days the group doesn't meet. The discussion works without them, but they're where much of the real change happens, because a wound named once in a meeting and never touched again tends to seal over. Encourage the men to do them, and consider opening each session by asking what came up in the week's readings.

faq.q: What if a man discloses abuse or a crisis during the study?
faq.a: Move out of curriculum mode and into care. Listen without prying for detail, take it seriously, do not promise confidentiality you cannot keep where safety is involved, and connect him with your pastor and, where appropriate, a qualified counselor. The study is formation, not therapy, and part of leading it well is knowing the line. If a man is in danger to himself or others, treat that as the emergency it is and get real help immediately.

faq.q: Several men in our group didn't grow up in church and feel they're starting from nothing as fathers of faith. Is this for them?
faq.a: Especially for them. The study assumes nothing and talks down to no one. Session five speaks directly to the man who is the first link in his family's chain of faith, with no example handed to him, and treats that as a calling, not a disqualification. A man doesn't need a religious childhood to begin. He needs to receive the Father's love and start where he is.

faq.q: Will this study make men feel like failures as fathers?
faq.a: It's built to do the opposite, though it doesn't flinch from naming real failure. Every session moves deliberately from the wound or the failure to grace, and the leader is asked to make that turn out loud every time, because conviction without grace turns into shame. The point isn't to grade a man's fathering but to free him, by the mercy of a Father who ran to him first, to father from grace rather than fear. If a man leaves heavier than he came, the turn to grace was skipped, and that's the one thing the leader mustn't let happen.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, men. For the next few weeks we're going to talk about something most of us have spent a lot of energy not talking about. Two ground rules. First, what is said in this room stays in this room, with the one exception that if someone is in danger, I will get help. Second, no fixing. When a man shares something hard, we don't rush to solve it; we receive it. I'll go first every week, because I'm not asking you to be more open than I'm willing to be.
facilitatorScript.transition: Let me take us from the wound to the only place this study can go, which is grace. Everything we just named, the absence, the failure, the silence, is real, and we're not going to pretend it's small. But none of it is the last word. The last word is a Father standing at the edge of a field, watching a road, ready to run. Let me read it again, and then let's sit quietly with it before we close.
facilitatorScript.close: Here's what I'm asking before next week. Don't turn tonight's conviction into one more thing to be ashamed of. Turn it toward the one thing God put his finger on. Take the practice seriously, even the part that feels awkward, and do the five short devotionals during the week, because that's where a lot of the real work happens. And if tonight opened something you need to talk about, find me afterward or this week. You don't have to carry it alone, and you were never meant to.

cadences.name: Five-week men's group
plan: One ninety-minute session a week for five weeks.
Open with food if you can. Men talk more openly around a table.
Keep the whole shape of each session, and don't skip the quiet room, where the real work often happens.
Send men home with the five devotional days, and open the next meeting by asking what came up during the week.
Plan a sixth, informal gathering a few weeks after the last session to check in on the one turn each man named.

cadences.name: Weekend retreat
plan: Sessions one and two on Friday evening and Saturday morning.
Sessions three and four on Saturday afternoon and evening, with long unstructured breaks for conversation.
Session five on Sunday morning, ending in worship and the blessing practice spoken aloud over one another.
Use the devotional readings as personal quiet time in the early mornings before the group sessions.
Build in real silence and time outdoors. The material needs room to settle, and men often think best while walking.

cadences.name: Ten-meeting slow track
plan: Split each session in two, the teaching and Scripture study one week, the discussion and quiet room the next.
Works best for early-morning or lunch meetings of forty-five minutes.
Spread the five devotional days across the two weeks each session covers, one every few days.
Open each second meeting with a short recap and the memory verse.
The slower pace suits men who need time between meetings for the truth to catch up with them.

bibliography.title: The Prodigal God
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: A short treatment of Luke 15 and the father who runs, including the older brother many religious men have never noticed they are. The backbone of session one.

bibliography.title: Life Together
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: On Christian community and the difference between the pretense of holiness and the real thing. Bracing on why we hide our failures from one another, and on listening as the first thing we owe a brother.

bibliography.title: The Cost of Discipleship
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: The source of the distinction between cheap grace and costly grace that session five draws on.

bibliography.title: A Long Obedience in the Same Direction
bibliography.author: Eugene Peterson
bibliography.note: On discipleship as unhurried, repeated, unspectacular faithfulness, the kind fathering asks for. The frame for presence in session two and the long view in session five.

bibliography.title: The Anxious Generation
bibliography.author: Jonathan Haidt
bibliography.note: A secular account of what the smartphone and social media are doing to childhood and attention. Read it for the symptom, and bring it under the gospel rather than beside it.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: The record of a man's wandering and return, shaped by a praying mother and a God who is the true Father. A witness to the long view in session five.

bibliography.title: The Freedom of Self-Forgetfulness
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: A short book arguing that in the gospel God's verdict comes before our performance, which grounds the account of the blessing in session four.

bibliography.title: Wild at Heart
bibliography.author: John Eldredge
bibliography.note: Widely read among men on the father wound and the question of whether a man has what it takes. Useful to start conversation; weigh its claims against Scripture rather than against our culture's picture of masculinity.

furtherReading: Luke 15 in full, the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the two lost sons, read in one sitting.
Deuteronomy 6, the Shema and the command to hand the faith down through the ordinary day.
Psalm 103, on the Lord who has compassion as a father shows compassion to his children.
Hebrews 12:1-13, on the discipline of a Father who is going somewhere with us.
Numbers 6:22-27, the priestly blessing, on what it sounds like to bless out loud, by name, with the face turned toward the one blessed.
2 Timothy 1, on the faith that lived first in Timothy's grandmother and mother and then in him.

glossary.definition: The lasting ache left by what a father failed to give, through absence, coldness, harshness or death. Not an excuse, but something a man has to name so he doesn't pass it on without knowing.

The spoken word of delight and belonging a father gives a child, unhooked from achievement. At its core are two sentences, "I delight in you" and "You're mine." A child who never hears it tends to spend a lifetime looking for it.

The picture at the center of Luke 15, where the father gives up his dignity and runs to embrace the returning son before the son can finish his rehearsed speech. The truest picture Jesus gives of God.

Keller's reading of Luke 15, that both the younger son who ran and the older son who stayed home keeping the rules are lost, and grace goes out to both. The dutiful man is often the one who has never felt his father's delight.
The ordinary gift of attention given in person over years. Distinguished here from provision, which can be given from a distance and is no substitute for it.

A father going back to a child after getting it wrong, naming the failure and asking forgiveness. The practice that keeps discipline from turning into wounding and shows what humble authority looks like.

Bonhoeffer's term for grace that costs nothing and changes nothing, forgiveness preached without repentance. A father who only performs having arrived hands his children something like it, a religion of appearances with no living root.
Fathering as planting trees whose shade you may not sit in, trusting that God gives the growth on a timeline you don't control and may not live to see.
Faith handed down a line of ordinary, named people, as from Lois to Eunice to Timothy, each faithful in their own stretch, with the harvest sometimes coming in a grandchild never met.
